prompt: Write an essay arguing for or against the claim that remote work is better than office work for software teams. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
The case for remote work on software teams rests on a simple observation: programming is an activity of sustained concentration, and the modern office is built to interrupt it. A developer holding a complex system in their head, tracing how a change in one module ripples through five others, is doing something fragile. A tap on the shoulder, a nearby sales call, or a spontaneous hallway debate can destroy twenty minutes of accumulated mental state in a second. Remote work, done well, gives engineers control over their attention, and attention is the scarcest resource a software team has. For that reason, and several that follow from it, remote work is the better default for software teams.

Start with the nature of the work itself. Software is unusual among collaborative professions in that nearly all of its artifacts are already digital and already shared. The code lives in a repository, the review happens in a pull request, the deployment runs through a pipeline, and the incident is diagnosed through dashboards and logs. Nothing about any of this requires physical proximity. An architect needs to visit the site and a surgeon needs to be in the room, but a developer's entire workplace fits through a network connection. When a team sits together in an office, they mostly sit side by side typing into the same tools they would use from home, wearing headphones to simulate the solitude they gave up by commuting.

The commute is itself a substantial argument. An engineer who spends ninety minutes a day traveling loses more than seven hours a week, close to a full working day, to an activity that produces nothing. Remote work returns that time, and people spend it on sleep, exercise, family, and sometimes on the work itself. A rested developer who started the day with a walk rather than a traffic jam writes better code. The benefit compounds over years in the form of lower burnout and longer tenure, and tenure matters enormously in software, where deep knowledge of a codebase takes years to build and walks out the door when someone quits.

Remote work also changes who a team can hire. An office-bound company recruits from the population willing to live within commuting distance of a particular building, often in one of the most expensive cities in the world. A remote company recruits from everywhere. That widens the pool by orders of magnitude and opens it to people the office model quietly excludes: parents who need flexible hours, people with disabilities for whom a daily commute is a serious barrier, and talented engineers who simply prefer to live near family in a smaller town. Better hiring is the highest-leverage improvement available to any software team, and geography is the largest artificial constraint on it.

The strongest objection is that offices produce something remote teams cannot: spontaneous collaboration, mentorship by osmosis, and the trust that comes from sharing lunch. This objection deserves respect, because the costs are real. Junior engineers do learn by overhearing, and relationships do form more easily in person. But the objection proves less than it seems. The serendipity of the office is unevenly distributed, favoring those who happen to sit near the right people and those comfortable interrupting others. Much of what gets called hallway collaboration is also undocumented decision-making, which leaves no record and excludes anyone who was not standing there.

Remote teams are forced to replace these informal channels with deliberate ones, and the replacements are often better. Decisions get written down in design documents and threads, which makes them searchable, reviewable, and available to the engineer who joins six months later. Mentorship becomes scheduled pairing sessions and thorough code review rather than a matter of luck. Writing things down is also a discipline that improves thinking, since a vague idea that survives a conversation frequently collapses when someone tries to put it in a paragraph. The open source world demonstrated long ago that this model works at scale. Linux, Postgres, and Python were built by people who rarely or never met, coordinating through text across every time zone.

None of this means remote work succeeds automatically. A team that goes remote while keeping office habits, filling calendars with video calls and expecting instant replies, gets the worst of both arrangements. Remote work demands investment in writing, in clear ownership, in asynchronous process, and in occasional in-person gatherings to build the trust that carries a team through hard disagreements. A few days together each quarter can do more for cohesion than a year of sharing a floor, because the time is spent intentionally on the things that benefit from presence.

The right comparison, then, is between remote work done deliberately and office work as it is ordinarily practiced. Measured that way, remote work gives software teams more focus, more time, better records of their own reasoning, and access to far more talent. The office offers convenience for managers and comfort for habit, and software teams can do better than that.
